workEn: The Secret History of the Mongols
title: 元朝秘史 §§257–259
titleEn: The Secret History of the Mongols — §§257–259: The Sartaul campaign
source: Mongγol-un niγuča tobčiyan (The Secret History of the Mongols), §§257–259, in the Ming Chinese-character phonetic transcription, as edited with a romanized reading by Shiratori Kurakichi 白鳥庫吉, 音訳蒙文元朝秘史 (Tokyo, 1943), itself based on the Ye Dehui 葉德輝 printed edition of 1905/1908; text taken from the Japanese Wikisource transcription, archived and verified against it character for character. Shiratori died in 1942, so the edition was public domain in Japan before the URAA date and was never restored in the United States. Section numbering (§) is the standard citation system. Romanization convention: Shiratori's, kept exactly as he prints it (γ, ġ, ṅ, ž, č, and the raised dot of γ̇). Translations are made fresh from the Mongolian, with the Ming interlinear Chinese glosses as the primary crib. No modern translation was consulted. langCode is null: there is no text-to-speech for Middle Mongol.
about: The campaign against the Sartaul, as the Secret History calls the Muslims of the west. Chinggis Qahan sends Jebe, Sübegetei and Toquchar ahead; Toquchar plunders where he was told to pass quietly and is removed from command. The Sultan Jalaldin and Qan Melig defeat Shigi-Qutuqu, are beaten in turn, and flee over the Shin River. The three sons are sent against Ürüngechi, where a question of command is settled by naming Ögödei, and Chinggis and Tolui take town after town and meet again. A note on the text: the Mongol is a Ming Chinese-character transcription, and the glosses in square brackets are the Ming glossators’ own; where the English departs from them or is unsure, the note says so.
draftNote: The Mongol readings follow Shiratori throughout; the English is a first drafting.

sentences.l: Hare year, Sartaul people-to, Arai-by crossing, when-mounting, Chinggis Qaγan lady-from Qulan lady-(object) taking, when-setting-out-on-campaign,
sentences.i: In the Hare year, as Chinggis Qahan mounted to cross by the Arai against the Sartaul people, he took Lady Qulan from among his wives as he set out on campaign,
sentences.n: The Ming gloss 免 on taulai is a miswriting of 兔 “hare”: the Hare year of the twelve-year cycle. Arai-jar is Arai plus the instrumental -jar (Ming 依着, “by way of”); a mountain Arai is named elsewhere, and daban “crossing” suggests a pass or ridge, but I cannot say which. Irgen-dür is “to the people”; the Ming 行 after a verb of going gives “against”. Qatun-ača is “from among the ladies” (Ming 內). Ajalarun is ajala- + -run; the stem is inferred from the Ming 征進 “set out to war”. The sentence runs on through the next units.

sentences.l: Younger-brothers-from Ödchigin Noyan-(object) great camp-in entrusting, mounted.
sentences.i: From among his younger brothers he put Ödchigin Noyan in charge of the great camp, and mounted.
sentences.n: Deġü-ner-eče is “from among the younger brothers” (Ming 弟(每自)); the ablative picks one out of a group. Tüšižü is tüši- “entrust” (Ming 委付着); the glossary also holds tüši- “stretch out the neck”, which does not fit here. Jeke aγ̇uruγ “great camp” is glossed 老營, the old or home camp. Nojan-(n)i: the (n) is Shiratori’s.

sentences.t: Žebe-ji maṅlai ilebe.

sentences.l: Jebe-(object) leading sent.
sentences.i: He sent Jebe at the head, in the van.
sentences.n: Maṅlai is “forehead”; the Ming 為頭 “as head, leading” shows it is used for “in front, at the head”. The pattern X-ji … ilebe “sent X” opens a chain of three (this unit and the next two): each man is the reserve of the one before.

sentences.i: As Jebe’s support he sent Sübegetei.
sentences.n: Gežige is “reserve, rear support” (Ming 後援). Žebe-jin is Jebe + the genitive, written -jin after a vowel stem.

sentences.n: The third link of the chain: van, then reserve, then reserve behind the reserve.

sentences.t: Ede γurban-i ilerün;
sentences.l: These three-(object), when-sending;
sentences.i: In sending out these three,
sentences.n: Ede “these” is the plural of ene (Ming 這(的每)); γurban-i is “three” + accusative. Ilerün is ile- “send” + the converb of time -rün. Here the Ming glosses the verb 敎去, “cause to go”; elsewhere 去 “go” alone, so “going” is another possible reading. The semicolon is Shiratori’s; the sentence goes on.

sentences.t: γadaγ̇un odču Sultan-u činana γarču bidan-i kürgeġülün qamsadqun keġežü ilebe.

morph.gloss: sultan, the Muslim ruler (Ming 囘囘王名 "name of a Muslim king"; a title) [囘囘王名(的)]
on the far side, beyond (postposition governing the genitive) [那廂]
stem extension of bida before case endings

sentences.l: Outside going, Sultan-of beyond going-out, us-(object) having-delivered, pincer-you-all saying, sent.
sentences.i: he sent them off with this order: “Go round by the outside, come out beyond the Sultan, and, once we have been brought up, close on him together.”
sentences.n: Doubtful in its last third. Činana “beyond” governs the genitive, so Sultan-u is “beyond the Sultan”; the Ming 囘囘王名 (“name of a Muslim king”) takes Sultan for a name, though it is a title. Bidan-i kürgeġülün is “having us delivered” (kürge- “bring to” + causative -ġül-), and qamsadqun is qamsa- + the plural polite imperative -dqun (Ming 夾攻您 “attack from both sides, you all”); the glossary’s qamsa- is “join, combine” (Ming 併), and here the Ming 夾攻 gives “attack from both sides”. I read it as an order to attack in a pincer when the main force arrives, but who brings whom is not settled by the grammar. Shiratori prints no quotation marks; I supply them in `i` only, since bidan-i “us” shows that Chinggis is speaking.

sentences.l: Jebe that going, Qan Melig’s towns passing, not disturbing, outside went-past.
sentences.i: Jebe, going that way, passed by the towns of Qan Melig without troubling them, keeping to the outside.
sentences.n: Ülü künden is “not stirring”: künde- is the glossary’s “disturb, touch, move” (reading uncertain; Ming 不動 “did not move or disturb”), and the sense “did not trouble (the towns)” is my reading. Nögčižüγ̇ü is nögči- “pass” (Ming 過去了) + a past ending -žüγ̇ü, seen also in jabužuγ̇ui; the ending is uncertain. Qān Melig is a title and a name (Ming 皇帝, (人)名), a Muslim lord; the forms Melig, Melig-ün, Melig-i follow.

sentences.l: That-one’s after Sübegetei likewise by-the-rule not disturbing went-past.
sentences.i: After him Sübegetei, in just the same way and as was proper, passed by without troubling them.
sentences.n: Mün (Ming 只) is “just, the very”, hence “likewise”; josu-γ̇ar (Ming 理依着) is “by the rule, by custom”. I take the pair as “in the same way, as was proper”. Nögčižüġü is the same verb as in the last unit, spelled with the front-vowel ġ here.

sentences.l: That-one’s after Toquchar, Qan Melig’s border towns seizing, farmers-(object) their plundered.
sentences.i: After him Toquchar seized the border towns of Qan Melig and plundered their farming people.
sentences.n: The contrast with the two quiet passes is the point: this is the offence punished in the last three units of §257. Qaγ̇ulžu is qaγ̇ul- “rush” (the glossary’s lemma); the Ming gives 據着 “occupying, seizing” here. Tarijačin is “tiller”: tarija- inferred from the Ming 種田 “cultivate”, plus the agent ending -čin. In-ü “their” stands after an accusative, which is unusual; the Ming 他的 reads it as “his, their”.

sentences.t: Qān Melig balaγad(i)-jan qaγ̇uldaγ̇a keġen daičin ködölžü Žalaldiṅ Soltan- dur neiležüġü.

morph.gloss: ruler, sovereign, khan (title, short form beside qaγan; here before a name) [皇帝]

sentences.l: Qan Melig, towns-his-own were-plundered saying, hostility moving, Jalaldin Sultan-to united.
sentences.i: Qan Melig, saying that his towns had been plundered, rose in hostility and joined Jalaldin Sultan.
sentences.n: Balaγad(i)-jan is “his own towns”: the (i) is Shiratori’s linking vowel, -jan the reflexive-possessive (Ming 自的行). Qaγ̇uldaγ̇a is qaγ̇ul- + passive -da- + a past ending -γ̇a; the analysis is uncertain, the Ming 被擄掠了 is “was plundered”. Daičin is “war, hostility”, glossed 反 “rebel”; ködölžü is “moving, stirring up”. The name Soltan- and its ending dur are split across two printed words (83–84); the Ming gives 王 and 行 “to”. No quotation marks are printed, so the complaint is indirect.

sentences.l: Jalaldin Sultan, Qan Melig the two, Chinggis Qaγan’s against, mounted.
sentences.i: Jalaldin Sultan and Qan Melig, the two of them, rode out against Chinggis Qahan.
sentences.n: Qojar “two” follows the pair it counts. Esergü (Ming 迎着) is “facing, meeting”; with the genitive Qaγ̇an-u it is “against Chinggis Qahan”, though the Ming’s “to meet” does not by itself say hostile.

sentences.i: Out in front of Chinggis Qahan, Shigi-Qutuqu led the way.
sentences.n: Urida “in front of” takes the genitive. Jabužuγ̇ui (Ming 行了) is jabu- “go” plus a past ending -žuγ̇ui whose analysis is uncertain; maṅlai “leading” as above.

sentences.l: Shigi-Qutuqu-with joining-battle, Jalaldin Sultan Qan Melig the two Shigi-Qutuqu-(object) overcoming, Chinggis Qaγan-to until overcoming,
sentences.i: Joining battle with Shigi-Qutuqu, Jalaldin Sultan and Qan Melig overcame Shigi-Qutuqu, and pressing the victory as far as Chinggis Qahan,
sentences.n: Baildužu is bai- “stand” + the reciprocal -ldu- + -žu: “standing against each other”, joining battle (Ming 對陣着). Daružu (Ming 勝着 “winning”) is daru- “press down, overcome”; I take it twice as “overcame … pressing on”. Šigi-Qutuqu-ji is the accusative: it is Shigi-Qutuqu who is beaten. Kürtele “until reaching” closes the pursuit.

sentences.l: At-the-coming, Jebe, Sübegetei, Toquchar the three, Jalaldin Sultan, Qan Melig the two’s from-behind entering,
sentences.i: As they came, Jebe, Sübegetei and Toquchar, the three, came in behind Jalaldin Sultan and Qan Melig,
sentences.n: Aisuqui-dur is aisu- “come” + the participle -qui + the dative-locative: “at the coming”. The subject of the coming is the two pressing Shigi-Qutuqu; the three then come in behind them. Qojar-un is “of the two”. Žebe and Sübeġetei here carry Shiratori’s commas, which I read as a list.

sentences.l: but them-(object) overcoming, having-killed,
sentences.i: and in their turn overcame them and slaughtered them,
sentences.n: Žiči (Ming 郤) is “but, in turn”, turning the tables. Kiduγ̇ad is kidu- “kill” (the glossary has kidu- “kill off”, Ming 盡殺; here the Ming has 殺 alone) + the perfective converb -γ̇ad.

sentences.l: Buqar, Semiskab, Udarar town-in them not making-join overcoming,
sentences.i: and in the towns of Buqar, Semiskab and Udurar overcame them without letting them join up,
sentences.n: Ming 城名 “town name” on each of the three. Neileġülün is neile- “join” + the causative: “make unite”; with ülü it is “not letting them unite”. I take it that the defeated were kept from regrouping in the towns. Balaγasun-dur is “in the town”; the plural sense of the three names rests on the list.

sentences.i: chasing them as far as the Shin River, as they were driven along,
sentences.n: Šin is a river (Ming 河名). Hüldežü (Ming 逐着) is hülde- “chase”, stem inferred. Jabuγdarun is jabu- “go” + the passive -γda- + -run: “when being made to go”, that is, driven (Ming 被行時).

sentences.l: Shin river-in plunging, when-entering, many Sartaul-their there Shin river-in perished.
sentences.i: plunging in as they entered the Shin River, many of their Sartaul perished there in the Shin.
sentences.n: Čübtüsčü: the Ming 猛投 “throw oneself in” fits plunging, though the glossary’s earlier gloss is “sink”. Oroqun bolun is “being on the point of entering” or “on entering”. Sartaγ̇ul(i)-jan is “their own Sartaul”: the people the Ming calls 囘囘. Süġebe-že is süġe- “be cut off” (Ming 絕了, stem inferred) + the past -be + -že “indeed”; they drowned.

sentences.l: Jalaldin Sultan, Qan Melig the two life-their clenching, Shin River upstream fled.
sentences.i: Jalaldin Sultan and Qan Melig, the two of them, with their lives clenched in their teeth, fled up the Shin River.
sentences.n: Qoroqun is glossed 刁着 “holding in the mouth”; the stem is uncertain, so the picture of “clenching their lives in their teeth” (barely escaping) is a literal reading, not a settled idiom. Öġede (Ming 逆) is “upstream, against the current”.

sentences.i: reached the Eke-Goroqan and the Ge’ün-Goroqan, and camped on the Baru’an Keger,
sentences.n: Two rivers (Ming 河名 each) and a place (Ming 地名). I do not translate the names: the glossary has eke “mother” and geġün “mare”, but as river names (Ming 河名 only) neither sense is safe, so I leave them. Baγ̇užu (Ming 下着) is “coming down, camping”.

sentences.i: and sent Bala of the Jalair to pursue Jalaldin Sultan and Qan Melig, the two of them.
sentences.n: Žalijartai is Žalijar + -tai “having, of”: the Jalair people (Ming 種名), here their man Bala. The same Bala is awaited in §259. Nekeġülün is neke- “pursue” (Ming 追襲) made causative: “having them pursued”.

sentences.i: He showed great favour to Jebe and Sübegetei, the two of them,
sentences.n: Sojurγažu (Ming 恩賜着) is “bestowing grace”. The favour is voiced in the next unit.

sentences.t: Žebe či Žirγoγ̇adai neretü büleġe. Taičuγ̇ud-ača irežü Žebe bolba-že či.

morph.gloss: Jirgo'adai, a man's name (Ming 人名) [人名]
past: was, used to be (as büleġe)

sentences.l: Jebe, you Jirgo’adai having-name was; Taichi’ud-from coming Jebe became-indeed, you.
sentences.i: “Jebe, you were named Jirgo’adai. You came from the Taichi’ud and became Jebe.”
sentences.n: Shiratori prints no quotation marks; I supply them in the translation because či “you” makes it a speech to Jebe. Neretü is nere “name” + -tü “having”; büleġe is the past “was, used to be”. Bolba-že is “became, indeed”, and the closing či repeats “you” for emphasis. The text takes for granted the story of how Jirgo’adai got the name Jebe.

sentences.i: As for Toquchar, he had seized the border towns of Qan Melig of his own accord, and so frightened Qan Melig.
sentences.n: Toqučar-i is a topic in the accusative: it is also the object of the last verb of the passage (the last unit of §257), where he is punished. Öġer-ün dura-γ̇ar (Ming 自己意依着) is “by his own will”, against the order given above to pass Melig’s towns without trouble. Daižiγ̇ulba is daiži- “fear” (stem inferred from the Ming 驚; the glossary’s daiži- is “turn hostile”, Ming 反, but here the Ming says fright) + the causative -γ̇ul-.

sentences.t: Žasaγ bolγan mököriġülüje keġen baražu

morph.gloss: to cut down, behead (verb; stem uncertain; Ming 斬) [斬咱]
to be finished, used up (verb) [了了着]

sentences.l: Law making, let-us-have-cut-down saying, finishing,
sentences.i: Saying that he would make it a law and have him cut down, and having done with that,
sentences.n: The subject is Chinggis. Žasaγ bolγan (Ming 法度 做) is “making it a rule”, that is, treating the act as a breach of discipline. Mököriġülüje is mököri- “cut down” (stem uncertain) + the causative + the hortative -je: “let us have him cut down”. Baražu (Ming 了了着) is bara- “be finished”; “having done with it” is my reading and doubtful: it may mean “having run out” of patience. The whole is given indirectly, since no quotation marks are printed.

sentences.t: žiči ülü mököriġülün maši duṅγodču čerig medekü-dēče in-ü ereġülüžü baγ̇ulba.

morph.gloss: to cut down, behead (verb; stem uncertain; Ming 斬) [斬]

he, she, it (third-person stem before the genitive) [他的]

sentences.l: but not making-cut-down, greatly rebuking, army knowing-from his blaming, removed.
sentences.i: he did not have him cut down after all, but rebuked him sharply and, blaming him for it, removed him from those who command the army.
sentences.n: Medekü-dēče is mede- “know, manage” (Ming 管的) + the participle -kü + the ablative -dēče: “from those who manage the army”, that is, the command. Baγ̇ulba: the Ming here has 削了 “cut away, stripped”, whereas the glossary glosses the same form “dismounted”; I take baγ̇ul- as baγ̇u- “come down” made causative, “bring down, demote”, but the stem is uncertain.

sentences.i: Then Chinggis Qahan turned back from Barula-Keger,
sentences.n: Tedüi (Ming 那遍 “that time”) opens the section: “thereupon”. Barula-Keġer is a place (Ming 地名), with the ablative -eče; the Ming 行 on it is not “to”. Qarižu is qari- “turn back, return”.

morph.gloss: plural (the linking vowel ü is Shiratori's)
instrumental: with (front-vowel form; the (i) is Shiratori's linking vowel)
Amui, a river (Ming 河名) [河名]
Ürüngechi, a town (Ming 城名) [城名]
town, city (noun; the final n is lost in print) [城子]

sentences.l: Jüchi, Cha’adai, Ögödei three sons-(object), right hand-of armies-with Amui river crossing, Ürüngechi town camp-at-you-all saying, sent.
sentences.i: He sent off his three sons, Jüchi, Cha’adai and Ögödei, with the words: “Cross the Amui River with the troops of the right hand and make camp before the city of Ürüngechi.”
sentences.n: Shiratori prints only the closing quotation mark (after baγudqun); I supply the opening, placing it where the command starts, after the sons are named. Baraγ̇un γar-un čeriġüd(i)-jer is “with the troops of the right hand”: the right wing (the -(i)- is a linking vowel, -jer the instrumental). Baγudqun (Ming 下營您, “pitch camp”) is baγu- “come down, halt, camp” + the plural polite imperative. Before a city I read it as “make camp before it”, not “take it”: the Ming 營 says camp, and in the sons’ report (next units) they have only “reached” the city. The Ming 您 shows the address is to all three. Ürüṅgeči and Amui are both glossed 城名 and 河名 only.

sentences.l: Tolui-(object), Iru, Isebür and-the-like many towns camp-at-you-all saying, sent.
sentences.i: He sent off Tolui with the words: “Make camp before the many towns, Iru, Isebür and the rest.”
sentences.n: Again only the closing mark is printed (after baγudqun); I supply the opening after Tolui-ji. Teriġüten is teriġü “head” + the plural possessive -ten, glossed 等 “and so on”; the glossary’s earlier remark that its sense is uncertain still holds, so “and the rest” is my reading. The plural polite imperative -dqun again, though only Tolui is named.

sentences.t: Čiṅgis Qaγan öġesün Udirar balaγasu baγ̇uba.

morph.gloss: Chinggis, the title borne by Temüjin from 1206 [太祖︀]

sentences.l: Chinggis Qaγan himself Udurar town came-down.
sentences.i: Chinggis Qahan himself took the city of Udurar.
sentences.n: Shiratori prints the town as Udirar here, Udarar in §257 and Udurar in §259; each time the Ming gives only 城名. I treat it as one town and write Udurar throughout. Baγ̇uba (Ming 下了) “came down” is read “took” of a town, but “camped before it”, as in the orders of §258 (Ming 下營), is also possible; the Ming 下了 does not settle it.

sentences.n: Öčižü is öči- “speak to a superior, report” (Ming 奏着; stem inferred); irerün is ire- “come” + the converb of time -rün. What they report follows in the next two units.

sentences.t: čeriġüd man-u bügüdbe. Ürüṅgeči balaγasu kürbe.

sentences.i: “Our troops are all together, and we have reached the city of Ürüngechi.
sentences.n: I begin the sons’ speech here because man-u “our” is first person. Bügüdbe is the doubtful word: the Ming 完全了 is “completed, whole”; I take it as “are all together, are complete”, with the stem bügüd- inferred. The closing quotation mark is printed at the end of the next unit.

sentences.t: Kun-ü-ġen üge-ġer jabuqun ba" keġen öčižü ireġesü

morph.gloss: who (interrogative pronoun; printed Kun-, but the Han 客 and the Ming 誰 give ken) [誰的自的(行)]
reflexive-possessive: one's own (front-vowel form, after a vowel)

sentences.l: Whose-own word-by going we, saying reporting, when-came.
sentences.i: Whose word are we to follow?” they said, as they came to report.
sentences.n: Kun-ü-ġen is ken “who” (printed Kun-, but the Han 客 reads ke-, and the Ming 誰 says “who”) + the genitive -ü + the reflexive -ġen: “whose own” (Ming 誰的自的). Ba (Ming 俺) is “we”, here after the verb. Jabuqun (Ming 行) is probably a participle in -qun, “the one going”. The question implies that the three could not agree who commanded; Chinggis’s answer in the next unit names Ögödei.

sentences.t: Čiṅgis Qaγan žarliγ bolurun: Öġödei-jüġen üge-ġer jabudqun keġežü ilebe.

Ögödei, a man's name [人名 自的行]

sentences.l: Chinggis Qaγan decree when-making: Ögödei-himself word-by go-you-all saying, sent.
sentences.i: Chinggis Qahan issued a decree: “Act on the word of Ögödei himself.” So saying, he sent them off.
sentences.n: Žarliγ bolurun is “when making a decree”, the house rendering “issued a decree”. Ögödei-jüġen is Ögödei + the reflexive -jüġen (Ming 自的行), “Ögödei’s own, Ögödei himself”. Jabudqun is the plural polite imperative: all three are bound. No quotation marks are printed here; the colon and the imperative show it is speech.

sentences.l: Then Chinggis Qaγan Udurar town making-enter,
sentences.i: Then Chinggis Qahan brought the city of Udurar to submission,
sentences.n: Oroγ̇ulžu is oro- “enter” + the causative -γ̇ul- + -žu; the Ming 敎投入着 “make it throw itself in” suggests “made it submit”, but the word could also mean “brought (his army) in”. The section starts the sequence of cities again from Udurar, which §258 ended on; I read §259 as the narrative picking up the thread.

sentences.n: The same pattern: balaγasun-ača … ködölžü … baγ̇uba. The three towns are those of §257, in the order Udurar, Semiskab, Buqar.

sentences.n: Küličen (Ming 等候) is küli- “wait for” (the glossary has küli- “wait”) with an ending -čen that I cannot parse. Bala is the Jalair man sent in pursuit in §257.

sentences.l: Altan-Gorqan’s ridge, Sultan’s summering-place summering, Tolui-to envoy sent.
sentences.i: on the ridge of Altan-Gorqan, the Sultan’s summer ground, where he spent the summer, and sent an envoy to Tolui.
sentences.n: Altan-Γorqan is a place (Ming 地名) and niriγ̇un is “back, spine”, glossed 脊: the ridge. Žusalaṅ is žun “summer” + -sa- + a place ending, “summering place” (Ming 過夏處); žusažu is “summering”. Whose summer it is, Chinggis’s or the Sultan’s, is not stated; I read Chinggis as spending the summer on the Sultan’s old summer ground.

sentences.t: Hon qalaγ̇un bolba.
sentences.l: Year hot became.
sentences.i: “The year has turned hot.
sentences.n: I begin the message to Tolui here; no quotation marks are printed at all in this passage except the closing one at the end of the message. Hon is “year” (Ming 年), so “the year has grown hot” is the plain sense: the summer heat has come.

sentences.t: Busud čeriġüd baγ̇ud-že

to come down, halt, camp (verb; the Ming 囘 "turn back") [囘 也者︀]

sentences.l: Others soldiers returned-indeed.
sentences.i: The other armies have come back to camp.
sentences.n: Baγ̇ud-že: the Ming 囘 means “turn back, return”, so I read baγ̇u- as “come down, halt, camp”; the ending -d is uncertain (plural or perfective). Busud is busu “other” + -d.

sentences.t: či bidan-dur neile" keġežü ileġesü

sentences.l: You us-to join” saying, when-sending.
sentences.i: You, join us!” With these words he sent the envoy off.
sentences.n: Closing mark printed at neile. Neile is the bare stem of neile- “join”, used as an imperative. Ileġesü is ile- “send” + the conditional -ġesü, “when he sent”; the main verb of the sentence comes in the last unit.

sentences.l: Tolui Chughcheren town having-broken, back descending having-come, Chinggis Qaγan-to joined.
sentences.i: Tolui broke the city of Chughcheren, then turned back, camped, came on, and joined Chinggis Qahan.
sentences.n: Qarin (Ming 囘) “back”, baγ̇užu “coming down, camping” and ireġed “having come” make a chain of three converbs before the main verb neilebe “joined”. The passage ends here.
